main_result: For every finite-dimensional complex vector space V, every a>=2 and every b>=a(a-1), the canonical map mu_{a,b,V}: Sym^b(Sym^a V) -> Sym^a(Sym^b V), induced by multiplication of invariant tensors, is surjective. Since complete reducibility holds over C, this gives a GL(V)-equivariant embedding Sym^a(Sym^b V) into Sym^b(Sym^a V) in the same range. The bound does not depend on dim V.
proof_strategy: The argument dualizes surjectivity to a statement about symmetric a-linear forms T on Sym^b V whose diagonal vanishes on products of b vectors, and then proves T=0 by induction on a. Step 1 uses the split binary form X^r+cY^r (r=a-1) to get T(x^rQ,...,x^rQ,t^rQ)=0 for products Q of m=b-r vectors. Step 2 applies the lowering operators D_{y_k,t} (which lower t-degree and raise y_k-degree) to turn t^r into t^b, and a Fischer-adjoint positivity lemma (p>q implies injectivity) peels them off to get T(x^rQ,...,x^rQ,t^b)=0. Step 3 applies the induction hypothesis for a-1 to the r remaining slots, using m>=r^2. Step 4 uses D_{x,v_i}^r with one shared variable x to remove the common power x^r, again using the degree inequality, so that T vanishes on pure powers; polarization then gives T=0. I checked the degree bookkeeping, the Fischer commutator identity ED-DE=N_U-N_Y, the coefficient extraction in Step 1, and the Step 4 inequality b-r+1>=r^2+1 (equivalent to b>=r(r+1)), and found them consistent. Parts that depend on the cited literature (Brion, Ikenmeyer, the CIM kernels, Problem 7.19) I could not verify.
hardest_part: The most delicate part is Step 4's bookkeeping: the r^2 lowering operators all raise the same x-block, and one must check at each application that the v_i-degree (at least m+1) exceeds the current x-degree (at most r^2-1). I checked this and it holds exactly under b>=r(r+1), but it depends on tracking which earlier operators hit the same block. The Fischer-inner-product lemma is short and I verified it, but the reader must recognize that the composition is injective only as a composite of degree-checked steps. The literature claims in the introduction are the part I could not check at all.

main_result: For every finite-dimensional complex V, every a>=2 and every b>=a(a-1), the canonical map mu_{a,b,V}: Sym^b(Sym^a V) -> Sym^a(Sym^b V) is surjective (equivalently A_b = R_b). Consequence: a GL(V)-equivariant embedding Sym^a(Sym^b V) into Sym^b(Sym^a V) exists in that range, by complete reducibility. The bound does not depend on dim V.
proof_strategy: The image of mu is the span of P^{⊗a} over products P of b vectors, so surjectivity reduces to: a symmetric a-linear form T on Sym^b V vanishing on the diagonal at all products is zero (Section 2, which I checked). Proposition 3.1 is proved by induction on a. Step 1 factors X^r + cY^r over C, which gives T(x^rQ,...,x^rQ,t^rQ)=0 for a product Q of m=b-r vectors. Step 2 applies r... specifically m derivatives D_{y_k}{t} to H_x = T(x^rQ,...,x^rQ,t^b), and the differential lemma (Fischer inner product, ED-DE = N_U - N_Y, which I verified) lets each step be inverted, giving H_x=0. Step 3 applies the induction hypothesis (a-1=r, with m >= r^2 >= r(r-1)) to the r-linear form Q_i -> T(x^rQ_1,...,x^rQ_r,t^b). Step 4 differentiates in x to remove the common x^r factor, with r^2 injective operators whose degree inequalities I checked, and concludes that T vanishes on pure powers, hence T=0. I could reconstruct every step of the proof and found no definite error; the gaps I list are about clarity and cited claims.
hardest_part: The least certain part is the claim that a polynomial identity in Step 2 (and the chained operator compositions in Steps 2 and 4) is inverted correctly at each stage, because the degree bookkeeping and the fact that intermediate polynomials are bihomogeneous must be tracked across several operators. I rechecked this and it holds. I could not independently verify the external claims used only for context: Problem 7.19 of Landsberg, the (5,5)/(6,6) kernel examples in CIM, and the 'sixth comparison' statement.

main_result: For integers a>=2 and b>=a(a-1) and any finite-dimensional complex V, the canonical map Sym^b(Sym^a V) -> Sym^a(Sym^b V) is surjective (uniformly in dim V). Corollary: for the same range there is a GL(V)-equivariant embedding Sym^a(Sym^b V) -> Sym^b(Sym^a V), obtained by complete reducibility from the surjection.
proof_strategy: Surjectivity is dualized: a functional on R_b = Sym^a(Sym^b V) corresponds to a symmetric a-linear form T on Sym^b V, and it suffices to show that T vanishing on the diagonal at all products of b vectors forces T=0. This is proved by induction on a. A binary factorization X^r + cY^r = prod(X - alpha zeta^j Y) with r=a-1 gives, from the linear coefficient in c, the vanishing T(x^rQ,...,x^rQ,t^rQ)=0. Lemma (sl2-type): D=sum Y_k d/dU_k is injective on bidegree (p,q) when p>q, via the identity ||Dh||^2-||Eh||^2=(p-q)||h||^2 with ED-DE=N_U-N_Y. Step 2 differentiates t-slot against y_1..y_m to strip Q from the last slot; Step 3 applies induction to the remaining r slots; Step 4 differentiates pure powers v_i^b into a shared variable x to remove the common power x^r and conclude T vanishes on pure powers. The bound b>=a(a-1) enters only as m=b-r>=r^2. I checked the commutator identity, the inner-product argument, the coefficient bookkeeping and the degree inequalities in Steps 2 and 4, and they hold.
hardest_part: The composition bookkeeping in Step 2 and Step 4: confirming that each intermediate polynomial has exactly the stated bidegree when Lemma is applied (which slot is the U-variable, which the Y-variable, and that no earlier operator touched the Y-variable), and the factor b!/(b-k)! and (b!/m!)^r constants. I verified these by hand, but the text leaves them terse, and the Fischer-inner-product adjointness D*=E is asserted rather than shown in detail.
